{"stage":"correction","question_id":"1B.3","answer":null,"critique":null,"corrected":{"question_id":"1B.3","answer":"Mexico had a substantial formal nuclear-safety architecture, but the evidence supports institutional capacity and procedures more clearly than consistently demonstrated effectiveness or direct López Obrador control. The legal framework assigns CNSNS responsibility for regulating, inspecting, licensing, monitoring, and enforcing nuclear, radiological, and physical safety, while CFE operates Laguna Verde. CNSNS had technical and operational autonomy and executive powers, but remained administratively subordinate to SENER; its greater de jure independence, knowledge-management plan, regulatory framework, and financial-resource position remained incomplete or constrained (BATCH-0002-E001, BATCH-0002-E002, BATCH-0002-E003, BATCH-0002-E006). The report also records government-funded plant operations, decommissioning and waste provisions, training, and 1,400 permanent employees in CFE’s Nuclear Corporate Coordination as of March 2022, though budget adequacy and presidential responsibility are not established (BATCH-0002-E008).

Implementation evidence is materially favorable but largely self-reported and pre-2023. CFE and CNSNS maintained safety-culture monitoring, self-assessment, external review, quality systems, corrective-action and root-cause processes, training and retraining, emergency procedures, spent-fuel controls, and post-Fukushima mitigation. The report says post-Fukushima progress was 98% and scheduled for completion by the end of 2023; it also records completed or implemented measures including spent-fuel-pool instrumentation, severe-accident procedures, and other mitigation systems, while FLEX Phase 3, some conclusion reports, and certain related actions remained incomplete or under development (BATCH-0002-E004, BATCH-0002-E007, BATCH-0002-E011). Mexico’s official support for IAEA safeguards, peer review, and nuclear safety is corroborating policy context, not proof of operational effectiveness (BATCH-0031-E001, BATCH-0031-E002, BATCH-0042-E002).

The record also shows concrete weaknesses. CNSNS documented multiple Laguna Verde non-compliances and imposed a fine on CFE; other sanction procedures were still being prepared or expected to begin in 2022. No inspections specifically focused on human and organizational factors were conducted at Laguna Verde during 2019–2021, although CNSNS reviewed human-factors controls through other mechanisms. Emergency exercises produced 78 findings, with follow-up rescheduled to 2022. Reported operational events involved equipment and design weaknesses, procedural omissions, human error, access-control failures, and maintenance problems. Reporting, investigation, root-cause analysis, and corrective-action mechanisms existed, but the supplied evidence does not establish that every weakness was finally corrected. Radioactive-waste storage also included a full temporary-storage warehouse and continuing capacity planning, without evidence here of resulting harm (BATCH-0002-E005, BATCH-0002-E009, BATCH-0002-E010, BATCH-0002-E012, BATCH-0002-E013).

During 2023, two radiological-security incidents provide direct target-year evidence of continuing exposure and regulatory response, but not a basis for attributing a specific custody failure to the president. In March, four Ir-192 sources were stolen from a licensed facility, recovered without reported radiological harm, and followed by regulatory inspection and approval of improved security measures; the IAEA recorded degradation of defence in depth. In October, organized crime stole a radiography camera containing a Category 3 Ir-192 source; the IAEA recorded degradation of defence in depth but no reported release, overexposure, contamination, injury, or continuing problem. The excerpts do not identify which controls failed or establish the adequacy of longer-term correction (BATCH-0040-E011, BATCH-0038-E002).

Broader cyber evidence is relevant only as adjacent catastrophic-risk governance, not as direct evidence of nuclear command-and-control. The 2022 Guacamaya breach exposed more than four million Sedena emails; reporting described inadequate protection, limited cybersecurity staffing, and cancelled equipment, while López Obrador acknowledged the breach but was reported not to address the security weakness or announce a remedy. Sedena later reported software updates, strengthened protections, and personnel training after 6,124 attack attempts through April 2023, while also reporting no federal-prosecutor complaint and reserving information about its internal investigation. Audits and Freedom House described unpatched systems and continuing military cybersecurity weaknesses, although the evidence does not establish that López Obrador personally directed the technical failures or subsequent measures (BATCH-0047-E010, BATCH-0008-E006, BATCH-0011-E005, BATCH-0026-E021). Qualifying evidence shows that financial authorities had made significant cybersecurity progress, while still facing resource, autonomy, oversight, and information-sharing gaps; this is peripheral and does not resolve the Sedena record (BATCH-0052-E024).

Overall, the evidence supports a functioning but imperfect nuclear-safety system with real inspection, staffing, training, corrective-action, emergency-preparedness, and accident-response mechanisms. It does not support describing those safeguards as uniformly effective, because independence and capacity gaps, non-compliances, incomplete preparedness work, recurring operational weaknesses, and 2023 radiological-security incidents remain documented. Nor does it establish that López Obrador personally enacted, funded, staffed, enforced, or corrected the nuclear safeguards, apart from limited evidence of his awareness and reported response concerning the broader Sedena cyber
